runs: Artificial intelligence is changing so fast that it is easy to get distracted by demos.

One week, everyone is talking about a chatbot that can write code. The next week, it is a swarm of agents moving around a canvas. Then it is a voice assistant booking meetings, summarizing calls, and sending follow-ups.
The surface keeps changing.
But underneath all of it, there is a much more important question:

b: What are the actual levels of AI capability, and where is all of this heading?

runs: That question matters for founders, product teams, investors, and everyday users. If you do not have a framework, it becomes very easy to confuse flashy interfaces with meaningful leaps in intelligence.

At Offboard, we spend a lot of time thinking about this because job search is one of the clearest examples of where AI should go next. A job search is not a single task. It is a messy, emotional, multi-week mission full of changing conditions, missed signals, deadlines, self-doubt, and constant reprioritization.
That makes it a great lens for thinking about the future of AI agents.
Here is the framework I keep coming back to.
This is the foundation.
Large language models brought us a new kind of software primitive: systems that can understand language, reason through problems, generate content, summarize, explain, and answer questions.
This first level is about knowledge and reasoning.
An AI at this level can:

items: answer a question
draft a message
summarize a document
brainstorm ideas
explain a concept
generate code or content

runs: This is the level most people first encountered with ChatGPT and similar products.
It was a huge breakthrough, but it is still mostly passive. The model waits for the user to ask for something.
The second level is where AI begins to
things, not just say things.
An agent combines intelligence with tool use. It can access software, browse the web, call APIs, update records, send drafts, read files, schedule actions, or manipulate a user interface.
This is where AI starts to feel useful in a more concrete way.
An agent at this level can:

items: research across multiple sources
update a CRM
draft and send outreach
modify a calendar or task list
read and analyze uploaded files
take action inside software tools

runs: This is the category most people mean when they say “AI agent” today.
The common mental model is:
LLM + tools = agent
That is a decent shorthand.
But this level is still often episodic. The agent handles a task or a session, then stops.
This is where things start to get much more interesting.
A persistent agent does not just complete a task and disappear. It stays connected to the problem over time.
It remembers the goal. It retains state. It can carry context across sessions. It does not need to be fully re-briefed every time.
This is the difference between:

items: “Help me draft this message”
“Help me keep making progress on this mission over the next six weeks”

runs: A persistent agent can:

items: track progress over time
remember what matters
carry unfinished work forward
maintain continuity across sessions
stay oriented around an outcome rather than a single prompt

runs: This is a major shift.
Most AI today is still task-based. Persistence is where AI starts to become longitudinal.

b: In simple terms: it stays with the problem.

runs: Persistence alone is not enough.
A system can remember context and still be dumb about what to do next.
The next level is adaptation: the ability to change strategy as conditions change.
An adaptive agent does not just keep going. It learns from what is happening and adjusts.
That means it can notice things like:

items: the current strategy is not working
a deadline is becoming urgent
the user is losing momentum
the environment has changed
a better path has opened up
the goal is the same, but the plan should change

runs: This is the level where AI begins to feel less like automation and more like judgment.

A lot of people describe the future of AI as “more autonomous.” That is part of it. But autonomy without adaptation is overrated. What matters is not that the system keeps moving. It is that it knows how to change course intelligently.
Once you have persistence and adaptation, the next leap is orchestration.
This is where multiple workflows, tools, or specialized agents work together under one higher-level objective.

We are already seeing early versions of this. Some products let you deploy multiple agents in parallel. Others split work across research, planning, writing, design, or code generation. In some cases, you can literally watch multiple agent cursors moving around a canvas or see several research threads being executed at once.
That is not just a gimmick.
It points to a future where AI is not one general helper, but a coordinated system of specialists.
An orchestrated system can:

items: divide work across specialized agents
run parallel research or execution paths
combine findings into one recommendation
coordinate multiple moving parts under one mission
prioritize which sub-problem matters most right now

runs: This is where the framework starts to move from useful to truly strategic.
An anticipatory system does not just respond to what has happened. It models what is likely to happen next and helps shape the path before problems fully emerge.
This is the beginning of something closer to a world model.
An anticipatory agent can:

items: infer which path has a higher chance of success
detect likely bottlenecks before they become obvious
simulate tradeoffs between different approaches
predict which actions matter most right now
recommend pivots before the user loses too much time

runs: This is a very different experience from basic AI assistance.

Instead of saying, “Here is the answer to your question,” it starts saying, “Given everything I know about your goal, your environment, and the outcomes so far, I think path B now has a better expected return than path A.”
That is a serious jump.

b: In simple terms: it chooses ahead.

runs: The final level in this framework is collective learning.
This is where the system improves not just from one user's history, but from patterns across many users, workflows, and outcomes.
At this level, the AI is no longer just helping a person in the moment. It is building a domain-specific intelligence layer.
A system with collective learning can:

items: learn which behaviors lead to the best outcomes
identify patterns across many users and cases
improve recommendations based on real-world feedback
create better playbooks over time
compound value as usage grows

runs: This is where real defensibility starts to appear.
It is also where the gap between generic AI wrappers and category-defining products gets much bigger.
A lot of AI product conversations get stuck because people mix up these levels.
A company will say they have an “agent,” but what they really have is a smart content generator with a few triggers.
Another company will show a multi-agent demo, but it still lacks persistence. It looks impressive in the moment, yet has no real continuity.
Another tool may remember context, but it does not adapt when the situation changes.
These are not all the same thing.
That is why having a framework matters.
It helps you ask better questions:

items: Is this system just intelligent, or is it agentic?
Is it agentic, or is it persistent?
Is it persistent, or is it adaptive?
Is it adaptive, or can it orchestrate?
Can it anticipate, or does it only react?
Does it learn across outcomes, or does it reset every time?

runs: That is how you separate novelty from actual capability.
One of my favorite analogies for this came from

Roz is interesting not because she can perform tasks. She is interesting because she locks onto a mission, adapts to a changing world, and keeps working toward the outcome through hundreds of sub-tasks.
She does not just need a new prompt every few minutes.
She stays oriented around the mission.
That is a useful benchmark for where AI is heading.

The best AI systems of the future will not just be smart tools. They will feel more like mission-aware systems that can stay grounded in an objective, adjust to changing conditions, and keep making progress over time.

That does not mean humans disappear from the loop. In many cases, quite the opposite. As AI becomes more powerful, trust, control, and judgment will matter even more. The systems that win will likely be the ones that feel collaborative, transparent, and aligned, not just hyper-automated.

text: What this means for the future of job search

runs: Job search is one of the clearest areas where this evolution matters.

The old process of applying cold through job boards is already under pressure. Recruiters are overloaded. Job seekers are overwhelmed. More of the process is fragmenting across referrals, communities, personal brands, direct outreach, AI-assisted applications, and internal talent networks.
In that world, a basic assistant is not enough.
Job seekers do not just need a chatbot that can rewrite a resume. They need help navigating a mission.
That mission includes:

items: choosing which roles are actually worth pursuing
deciding where to spend limited time and energy
adjusting strategy based on traction or lack of traction
preparing for interviews
managing emotional momentum
balancing ideal roles against financial urgency
keeping all of the moving parts organized across weeks or months

runs: That is why we believe the future is not just AI assistance. It is adaptive, persistent AI that can help users manage a real-life transition.
AI is not evolving in one straight line.
It is expanding across several dimensions at once: intelligence, action, persistence, adaptation, coordination, anticipation, and learning.
But if I had to simplify the path, I would say it like this:

items: means AI knows.
means AI acts.
means AI stays with the problem.
means AI changes strategy.
means AI coordinates many moving parts.
means AI sees around corners.
means AI gets better across outcomes.

runs: That is the ladder.

And the products that matter most in the next few years will probably not be the ones with the flashiest demo. They will be the ones that move meaningfully up that ladder in ways that solve real human problems.
At Offboard, that is the direction we are building toward.
Not just AI that answers.

b: AI that stays with the mission.
